In their small town near Ludhiana, Jasleen and Rajni had been the loudest pair at every wedding. Rajni did impressions of the aunties that made even the aunties laugh.
This winter, Jasleen noticed Rajni had stopped doing impressions. She'd stopped coming to kabaddi practice too, and her phulkari lay half-finished on the charpai.
At the gurdwara langar, Rajni muttered about 'the factory lot' from the new industrial area. 'They're all thieves. They're why the town's ruined. Every single one.'
'Rajni, Pinky's husband works there.'
'Then he's part of it.'
When Jasleen stayed over, she woke at three to see Rajni's face lit blue by her phone, scrolling. In the morning Rajni barely spoke about anything except 'them'.
Jasleen lay awake, trying to remember when Rajni last laughed at something that wasn't cruel.

qa.q: What did Rajni leave half-finished on the charpai?
qa.a: Her phulkari lay half-finished on the charpai.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling as she lay awake?
qa.a: Jasleen was worried and sad, missing the old, funny Rajni and troubled by her new cruelty.

qa.q: How could Jasleen respond to the warning signs she has noticed?
qa.a: She could stay close and kind, invite Rajni back to kabaddi or embroidery, calmly disagree with blaming everyone, and seek a trusted elder's advice.

qa.q: How might Pinky's husband feel if he heard Rajni call him 'part of it'?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and unfairly judged, blamed simply for where he works.

Xin had shared a flat with Sofia in Madrid for two years, and she used to be the funniest person Xin knew: terrible puns, cartoons on the fridge, tears at dog videos.
This spring the cartoons stopped. Sofia stayed up till four most nights, face lit blue, and in the mornings she spoke in absolutes. "They're all the same." "Every one of them is lying." At dinner, whatever the topic, rent, exams, a late train, the talk ended at the same group of people, as if they caused everything. She had quit her dance class. She no longer watched films with Xin.
When Xin mentioned a kind neighbour from that group, Sofia sneered. "One exception proves nothing."
That night Xin couldn't sleep either. Instead of arguing, Xin knocked on Sofia's door at eleven with two mugs of hot chocolate. "I miss you. The punny one. Can we just talk?"

qa.q: Till what time did Sofia stay up most nights?
qa.a: Till four most nights.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling the night after Sofia sneered?
qa.a: Xin felt worried and sad, unable to sleep, missing the funny, gentle friend.

qa.q: Why is Xin's hot chocolate and 'I miss you' a wise approach?
qa.a: It reaches for the friendship instead of arguing, which keeps Sofia connected to someone outside the feed.

qa.q: What might Sofia be going through as her world narrows?
qa.a: She is likely exhausted and consumed by anger, losing dance and films while one group becomes the answer to everything.

grounding: A flatmate notices a once funny, gentle friend speaking in absolutes, scapegoating one group, staying online at night and losing other interests.

In the engineering college canteen, Bhupen noticed it before anyone said it aloud: Tanuja had changed.
In first year she drew caricatures of the professors and fed biscuits to the canteen cat. Now she sat hunched over her phone reading threads, and every conversation bent to one topic. The hostel water shortage? "Because of them." The failed lab experiment? "Them again." She said "all of them" and "always" a lot.
Last week the robotics club she had founded met without her. She said she had "more important things to fight". Her eyes were red-rimmed from nights online.
Today, when a junior mentioned a friend from that group, Tanuja laughed coldly and used a name Bhupen had only ever seen in the worst comment sections.
Bhupen felt his stomach drop. After class he waited for her by the cycle stand. "Hey. The robotics lot miss you. I miss your caricatures. Chai?"

qa.q: What club had Tanuja founded?
qa.a: The robotics club.

qa.q: What did Bhupen feel when Tanuja used the name from comment sections?
qa.a: He felt shocked and worried, his stomach dropping at how much his friend had changed.

qa.q: What is wise about Bhupen's invitation at the cycle stand?
qa.a: It reconnects Tanuja with what she loved and with friends, without starting an argument she would defend against.

qa.q: What might Tanuja be losing as the scapegoating grows?
qa.a: She is losing sleep, her robotics club and her playful side, as anger crowds out everything she used to enjoy.

grounding: A classmate notices a formerly playful friend blaming one group for everything, sneering at them, staying online at night and dropping her interests.

Dear Ankita,
I've written this three times and deleted it. I'm sending it this time because I love you and I'm scared.
You used to be the gentlest person in our group. You cried at that film about the elephant. You made everyone laugh at the Lohri party with your impressions.
These last months, when we talk, it's always the same: one group of people, and how they ruin everything. Rent, jobs, traffic, even your cousin's wedding being delayed. You say "always" and "every single one". Last week you posted that joke comparing them to insects. You never used to talk about anyone like that.
You told me you're up till three most nights reading. You skipped Mehak's birthday. You haven't sketched since winter.
I'm not writing to fight. I just want to know what's really frightening you, because I think something is. Call me whenever. Tonight, if you want.
Gurleen

qa.q: What did Ankita post last week?
qa.a: That joke comparing them to insects.

qa.q: What is Gurleen feeling while writing this letter?
qa.a: Gurleen feels scared and loving, having written it three times, worried about how much Ankita has changed.

qa.q: What makes Gurleen's letter a good way to reach Ankita?
qa.a: It names specific changes gently, avoids a fight, and asks what is really frightening Ankita, keeping the door open.

qa.q: What might Ankita feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Ankita may feel defensive at first, but also seen and cared for by a friend who remembers a gentler Ankita.

grounding: A friend writes to someone once gentle who now scapegoats one group, speaks in absolutes, stays up online and has dropped old interests.

I see him in the lab, dark circles, not even opening his code. He doesn't play football anymore, doesn't come for our Friday biryani. I'm scared for him. I don't want to lose him, but I don't know how to talk to him without it turning into a fight."
